title: Compliance, Data Protection, and Securing AI Workloads
bodyMarkdown:
## Shared responsibility, and why a provider certificate is not yours

Compliance on Google Cloud is shared. The [shared responsibility and shared fate documentation](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/security/shared-responsibility-shared-fate) splits duties by service model:

- **IaaS** (Compute Engine, Cloud Storage): Google secures the underlying infrastructure; you carry most application, configuration, and data-protection duties.
- **PaaS** (App Engine, GKE): Google takes on more, but you still share application-level controls and IAM management and remain responsible for your data and client protection.
- **SaaS** (Google Workspace): Google owns most controls; you remain responsible for access controls and the data you put in.
- **FaaS:** like SaaS, Google manages the platform and you control access and data.

For PCI DSS, HIPAA, and GDPR the responsibilities are further split in published responsibility matrices, which you should consult. The practical consequence: Google's audit reports and certifications attest to Google's controls over its infrastructure and services. They do **not** make your application compliant, so a SaaS startup asked for a SOC 2 report still needs its **own** audit covering its application, access management, change management, and operations. Google's report is evidence you can inherit controls from, not a substitute.

"Shared fate" is Google's extension of the idea: secure blueprints and landing-zone guidance, Security Command Center Premium, Organization Policies, and Confidential Computing to help you stay compliant, plus a cyber-insurance program.

## Regimes mapped to controls

| Regime / data type | What drives the design | Typical controls |
|---|---|---|
| **HIPAA** (PHI) | Execute a BAA, use only covered services, no PHI in unsupported places | CMEK, Data Access audit logs, least-privilege IAM, VPC-SC, restricted log sinks |
| **PCI DSS** (card data) | Minimize where raw PANs exist to shrink scope | Sensitive Data Protection tokenization, network segmentation, logging, key management |
| **GDPR** (EU personal data) | Lawful processing, data-subject access and erasure, residency choices | Data processing terms (DPA), location constraints, Sensitive Data Protection discovery and classification |
| **Data sovereignty** | Data location **and** who can access it | Assured Workloads control package plus location org policy, key control (CMEK/EKM) |
| **SOC 2 / audits** | Evidence of controls over time | Audit logs to an immutable restricted sink, SCC posture reports, change records |

### HIPAA specifics

The [HIPAA documentation](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hipaa) states the rules that questions probe. You must determine whether you are a Covered Entity or Business Associate and, if so, accept the **BAA** through the "Privacy compliance and records for Google Cloud" support page. The BAA covers Google's infrastructure and 200+ services, including BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Cloud SQL, Compute Engine, GKE, Cloud KMS, Secret Manager, Logging and Monitoring. You may **not** use unsupported services or pre-GA offerings with PHI, and the customer must configure everything else. Documented restrictions include: do not store PHI in resource metadata or monitoring labels, avoid PHI in Identity Platform custom attributes and in Cloud Build configuration, and keep Speech-to-Text data logging disabled. Signing the BAA is necessary and not sufficient; the controls above are still yours to apply.

## Sensitive Data Protection

Sensitive Data Protection (formerly Cloud DLP; the API is still the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API) has four capabilities, per the [overview](https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/sensitive-data-protection-overview):

- **Discovery:** data profiles across an organization to find where sensitive data lives.
- **Inspection:** deep scans of specific resources for sensitive instances (infoTypes).
- **De-identification:** masking, redaction, bucketing, date shifting, and tokenization.
- **Risk analysis:** re-identification risk in structured data.

It can scan BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Cloud SQL, and Vertex AI.

The [pseudonymization documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/pseudonymization) is the key to the PCI question. Three methods are available: **deterministic encryption (AES-SIV)**, reversible but not preserving length or character set; **format-preserving encryption (FPE-FFX)**, reversible and preserving both; and **cryptographic hashing (HMAC-SHA-256)**, one-way. All three give **referential integrity**: the same key and context tweak always produce the same token, so analytics joins still work. Use **Cloud KMS wrapped keys** (recommended), not raw unwrapped keys in production. The page lists reducing compliance scope for PCI DSS and HIPAA and protecting development environments as intended use cases. So for "replace PANs with surrogate values that still join," the answer is de-identification with format-preserving tokenization, not simply encrypting the whole table or relying on firewall rules.

| Need | Technique |
|---|---|
| Hide value permanently, no joins | Redaction or masking |
| Joins and analytics on tokens, one-way | HMAC-SHA-256 hashing |
| Joins plus ability to reverse for authorized workflows | AES-SIV or FPE-FFX with a KMS-wrapped key |
| Token must look like the original (length, digits) | FPE-FFX |
| Coarsen numeric or date detail | Bucketing, date shifting |
| Know where sensitive data is | Discovery profiles |

## Residency and sovereignty

Two controls, with different jobs. The [Assured Workloads overview](https://cloud.google.com/assured-workloads/docs/overview) describes a sovereign data and access boundary with residency, access, and personnel controls. Packages fall into **regional data boundaries** (EU, US, UK, Canada, Australia and others), **regulatory data boundaries** (FedRAMP Moderate/High, CJIS, IL2/IL4/IL5, ITAR, IRS 1075, healthcare), and **Sovereign Controls by Partners**. It enforces them with Organization Policy constraints at the **folder** level, restricts storage location, lets you control which Google personnel handle support through Assured Support (with Enhanced or Premium support plans), supports CMEK, Cloud KMS, or Cloud EKM depending on package, and monitors for violations. Access Approval, Access Transparency, and Key Access Justifications add visibility.

`constraints/gcp.resourceLocations` is narrower. The [defining locations page](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/defining-locations) says it limits where **new** resources are created for supported services, and is **not** a data residency commitment. Therefore: a requirement that data **and the personnel who can access it** stay in the EU maps to **Assured Workloads (EU Regions and Support) plus** the location constraint, not to a single EU multi-region bucket and not to the constraint alone.

## Securing AI workloads

Generative AI adds attack surfaces: prompt injection, jailbreaks, harmful content, malicious URLs in prompts or responses, and sensitive-data leakage. [Model Armor](https://cloud.google.com/model-armor/docs/overview) screens both **prompts and responses**:

- **Prompt injection and jailbreak** detection, with blocking when detected.
- **Malicious URL** detection (up to 256 URLs per request).
- **Responsible AI filters** for hate speech, harassment, sexually explicit and dangerous content.
- **Sensitive Data Protection integration** to flag PII, financial data, and credentials.
- **Document screening** (PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, CSV, TXT, up to 4 MB) and image screening in Preview.

Behavior is controlled by **templates** with confidence thresholds: **High**, **Medium and above**, or **Low and above** (more false positives). Google recommends separate templates for input and output because their risk profiles differ. **Inspect only** logs detections without blocking, which is the safe way to tune; **Inspect and block** enforces. **Floor settings** set organization-wide minimum protections across all templates. Model Armor is stateless and integrates with Vertex AI, Gemini Enterprise, Apigee, GKE via Service Extensions, and MCP servers.

Around the model, reuse the controls from earlier modules: least-privilege IAM per agent or service account, CMEK where required, secrets in Secret Manager, a VPC-SC perimeter for the projects (confirm each AI service you use is supported inside a perimeter), audit logs, and Binary Authorization for custom serving containers. Model Armor is the only one of these that understands **prompt and response content**; an edge WAF or DDoS control does not.

## Audits and evidence

Auditors want evidence over time. Enable the right [audit logs](https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit) (Data Access for PHI and PII, since it is off by default except BigQuery), route them through an org-level aggregated sink to a restricted destination, and use Security Command Center to monitor posture against frameworks such as NIST, HIPAA, and PCI-DSS.

## Common mistakes and anti-patterns

- **Presenting Google's SOC 2 as your SOC 2.**
- **Treating the BAA as compliance.** It is the contractual start; covered services, CMEK, logging, and access control are still required.
- **Using non-covered or pre-GA services for PHI**, or putting PHI in labels and metadata.
- **Using `gcp.resourceLocations` alone for sovereignty**, or assuming it relocates existing resources.
- **Encrypting a whole PAN column** when tokenization with preserved joins would remove it from scope.
- **Raw, unwrapped keys for tokenization** instead of Cloud KMS wrapped keys.
- **Putting an LLM behind only a network firewall.** Prompt injection arrives in perfectly legitimate HTTPS requests.
- **Launching Model Armor in block mode untested.** Tune thresholds in inspect-only mode first.
- **No data inventory.** You cannot honor GDPR access and erasure requests for data you cannot find; run discovery.

## Exam tips

- **Provider cert is not your cert:** Google's SOC 2 covers its infrastructure; you still need your own SOC 2 for your application and operations.
- **HIPAA recipe:** sign the BAA, use only covered services, enable Data Access logs, protect with CMEK and least privilege; keep PHI out of labels and metadata.
- **PCI scope reduction:** Sensitive Data Protection de-identification with format-preserving tokenization using KMS-wrapped keys; tokens still support analytics joins.
- **GDPR:** DPA plus location constraints, and Sensitive Data Protection discovery to find personal data for access and erasure requests.
- **Sovereignty with personnel controls:** Assured Workloads (for example EU Regions and Support) plus `gcp.resourceLocations`; the constraint alone is not a residency commitment.
- **Gen-AI prompt and response protection:** Model Armor, optionally with Sensitive Data Protection; tune in inspect-only mode first and use floor settings for org baselines.
- **Naming:** Cloud DLP is now Sensitive Data Protection; the API name is unchanged.
- **Evidence:** immutable, restricted audit sinks and SCC posture reporting support audits.
